stim-0001.text: A researcher randomly assigned 60 college students to one of two groups. Both groups studied the same list of 20 words for 15 minutes. One group took three short practice quizzes on the words; the other group re-read the list three times. One week later, all students wrote down as many words as they could remember.

stim-0002.text: Dr. Mbeki studied how the timing of study sessions affects memory. She randomly assigned 120 college students to one of two groups. All students studied the same list of 30 words for a total of 30 minutes. The massed group studied for 30 minutes in one session. The distributed group studied for 10 minutes on each of three consecutive days. Each student was tested on recall of the words 1, 7, or 14 days after the last study session. The graph shows the mean number of words recalled.

stim-0003.text: Dr. Okoye studied whether talking on a phone affects what walkers notice. She randomly assigned 200 college students to walk across a campus square. One group of 100 students talked on a phone while walking. The other group of 100 students walked without a phone. A person in a clown costume rode a unicycle along the walkers' path. After each walk, students were asked whether they had seen anything unusual.

table.title: Students Who Noticed the Unicycling Clown

stim-0004.text: Dr. Ncube studied how sleep affects problem solving. She randomly assigned 90 high school students to sleep for 8 hours, 6 hours, or 4 hours in a sleep lab. The next morning, each student solved 20 math problems. The graph shows the mean number of problems solved correctly in each group.

stim-0005.text: Dr. Varga studied how long it takes for people to see dim light after entering a dark room. Each of 40 adults sat in a dark room and was tested after 0, 10, and 20 minutes. At each test, the researcher lowered the brightness of a small light until the adult could detect it only half of the time. The table shows the mean light intensity at that point, in arbitrary units.

table.title: Mean Dimmest Light Intensity Detected Half of the Time

dq-0001.question: Every time Priyanka finishes her chores before dinner, her parents let her skip washing the dishes that night. Priyanka now finishes her chores early almost every day. Which of the following best explains the change in Priyanka's behavior?
dq-0001.explanation: Correct: B. Removing an unpleasant task (washing dishes) after the behavior makes the behavior more likely, which is negative reinforcement.

distractor_notes.A: Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant; nothing is added here.
distractor_notes.C: Punishment makes a behavior less likely; her chore behavior increased.
distractor_notes.D: Negative punishment removes something pleasant to decrease a behavior.

dq-0002.question: Which of the following is the best example of the phonological loop at work?
options: Jordan pictures the route from his house to school to estimate the distance.
Lena repeats a new phone number under her breath until she can type it in.
Marcus remembers how to ride a bike after years without practice.
Ana recalls the details of her tenth birthday party.
dq-0002.explanation: Correct: B. The phonological loop holds and rehearses verbal and auditory information in working memory, as when repeating a number to keep it active.

distractor_notes.A: Mental images of a route use the visuospatial sketchpad.
distractor_notes.C: Riding a bike is a procedural (implicit) memory.
distractor_notes.D: Personal events are episodic long-term memories.

dq-0003.question: After a head injury, Tomas can see objects clearly but cannot recognize familiar faces. Which region labeled in the figure is most likely damaged?
dq-0003.explanation: Correct: C. Region Y is the temporal lobe, which includes an area involved in recognizing faces.

distractor_notes.A: W is the frontal lobe, linked to planning and movement.
distractor_notes.B: X is the parietal lobe, linked to touch and spatial processing.
distractor_notes.D: Z is the occipital lobe; damage there would impair basic vision, but Tomas sees clearly.

dq-0004.question: What is the independent variable in this study?
options: The number of words each student recalled one week later
Whether students took practice quizzes or re-read the list
The 15 minutes students spent studying the list
The college students who took part in the study
dq-0004.explanation: Correct: B. The researcher manipulated the study method (quizzes or re-reading), so it is the independent variable.

distractor_notes.A: Words recalled is the measured outcome, the dependent variable.
distractor_notes.C: Study time was held constant for both groups.
distractor_notes.D: The participants are the sample, not a variable.

dq-0005.question: Which of the following concepts is best supported by the results shown in the graph?
dq-0005.explanation: Correct: A. Students who practiced retrieving the words recalled more of them, which is the testing effect.

distractor_notes.B: The study did not compare words by their position in the list.
distractor_notes.C: No earlier learning interfered with the new list.
distractor_notes.D: The students' internal states were not varied.

dq-0006.question: Which of the following is a defining feature of panic disorder?
options: Recurring, unexpected episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms
Persistent fear of being judged in social situations
Unwanted repetitive thoughts paired with ritual behaviors
Flashbacks and nightmares following a traumatic event
dq-0006.explanation: Correct: A. Panic disorder involves repeated, unexpected panic attacks with physical symptoms such as a racing heart.

distractor_notes.B: Describes social anxiety disorder.
distractor_notes.C: Describes obsessive-compulsive disorder.
distractor_notes.D: Describes posttraumatic stress disorder.

dq-0007.question: A smudge covers the middle of one word in the sentence "The cat chased the mouse across the kitchen floor." Kiran reads the whole sentence quickly and does not notice the smudge. Which of the following best explains why Kiran reads the word so easily?
dq-0007.explanation: Correct: A. Kiran uses expectations and the surrounding context to interpret the smudged word, which is top-down processing.

distractor_notes.B: Bottom-up processing builds perception from the raw features alone, without relying on context.
distractor_notes.C: Constancy keeps an object's properties stable as viewing conditions change.
distractor_notes.D: Selective attention is about focusing on one stimulus and ignoring others.

dq-0008.question: Mateo is talking with a friend in a loud, crowded cafeteria and cannot follow the other conversations around him. From across the room, he suddenly hears someone say his name. Which of the following best explains what happened?
dq-0008.explanation: Correct: C. Mateo focuses on one conversation and filters out the rest, yet his own name still pulls his attention away.

distractor_notes.A: Change blindness is failing to notice a change in a visual scene.
distractor_notes.B: Inattentional blindness is missing a visible object while attending to something else; nothing is missed here.
distractor_notes.D: A perceptual set is a readiness to perceive in a certain way; it does not describe filtering sound.

dq-0009.question: In a photograph, two parallel railroad tracks appear to move closer together as they stretch toward the horizon. This helps viewers judge how far away the horizon is. Which of the following depth cues does the photograph use?
dq-0009.explanation: Correct: B. Parallel lines that seem to meet in the distance provide the monocular cue of linear perspective.

distractor_notes.A: Interposition is one object partly blocking another.
distractor_notes.C: Retinal disparity is a binocular cue and cannot be created by a flat photograph.
distractor_notes.D: Texture gradient is the way texture becomes finer with distance; the stem describes converging lines.

dq-0010.question: Ana watches a friend walk away down a long hallway. The image of her friend on Ana's retina gets smaller and smaller, but Ana does not think her friend is shrinking. Which of the following best explains Ana's perception?
dq-0010.explanation: Correct: D. Ana keeps perceiving the friend's size as unchanged even though the retinal image shrinks, which is size constancy.

distractor_notes.A: Apparent movement is seeing motion when there is none, such as in a series of still images.
distractor_notes.B: Relative size is a depth cue comparing objects of known size; it does not explain a stable perception of one object.
distractor_notes.C: Closure is filling in gaps to see a complete figure.

dq-0011.question: Which of the following Gestalt principles best explains why most people looking at the figure see the dots as groups?
dq-0011.explanation: Correct: B. The dots in each cluster are close together, so the viewer groups them by proximity.

distractor_notes.A: Closure is perceiving a complete shape from an incomplete one; no gaps in a shape are filled here.
distractor_notes.C: Similarity groups items that look alike, but all of the dots are identical.
distractor_notes.D: Figure and ground separates an object from its background, not groups of objects.

dq-0012.question: After watching several news reports about plane crashes, Dr. Nguyen's neighbor decides that driving across the country is safer than flying. Statistics show that flying is much safer per mile traveled. Which of the following best explains the neighbor's decision?
dq-0012.explanation: Correct: A. Vivid, easily remembered crash stories make the risk of flying seem more likely than it is.

distractor_notes.B: The representativeness heuristic judges by how well something matches a prototype, not by how easily examples come to mind.
distractor_notes.C: Functional fixedness is seeing an object only in its usual use.
distractor_notes.D: The gambler's fallacy is believing that past random events change the odds of future ones.

dq-0013.question: Farah pays $15 for a movie ticket. Thirty minutes into the film she is bored and would rather leave, but she stays because she does not want to waste the money she paid. Which of the following is most consistent with Farah's decision?
dq-0013.explanation: Correct: D. Farah lets money that is already spent and cannot be recovered guide her choice, which is the sunk-cost fallacy.

distractor_notes.A: The gambler's fallacy is a belief about random outcomes, such as a coin flip being "due."
distractor_notes.B: The representativeness heuristic compares something to a typical example.
distractor_notes.C: Framing is the way wording changes a choice; the same wording is not at issue here.

dq-0014.question: A hiker needs to tighten a loose screw on a backpack but has no screwdriver. A friend suggests using a coin, but the hiker says, "A coin is only for paying for things," and keeps searching. Which of the following best describes the hiker's thinking?
dq-0014.explanation: Correct: C. The hiker can only see the coin in its usual role as money, which blocks a new use for it.

distractor_notes.A: A mental set is repeating a strategy that worked before; the hiker is not reusing a past solution.
distractor_notes.B: Convergent thinking narrows many ideas to one correct answer.
distractor_notes.D: Divergent thinking generates many ideas, which the hiker is not doing.

dq-0015.question: A young child has only seen small pet dogs and calls a horse a "big dog." After her father explains it is a horse, the child creates a new mental category for horses. Which of the following processes best describes the creation of the new category?
dq-0015.explanation: Correct: B. The child changes her schema by building a new category because the existing one did not fit, which is accommodation.

distractor_notes.A: Assimilation fits new information into an existing schema, as when she first called the horse a dog.
distractor_notes.C: Priming is an earlier cue influencing a later response.
distractor_notes.D: A mental set is a habit of using a previously successful strategy.

dq-0016.question: Dr. Adeyemi tells one group of patients that a surgery has a 90% survival rate. She tells a second group that the same surgery has a 10% death rate. The first group is much more willing to have the surgery. Which of the following best explains this result?
dq-0016.explanation: Correct: D. The same facts led to different choices because they were worded as a gain in one case and a loss in the other.

distractor_notes.A: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution.
distractor_notes.B: The representativeness heuristic judges by similarity to a prototype.
distractor_notes.C: Priming is an earlier stimulus influencing a later response, not the wording of one message.

dq-0017.question: Tanvir easily describes his tenth birthday party to a friend, including blowing out the candles, the cake flavor, and the gift his cousin gave him. Which of the following types of memory is Tanvir mainly using?
dq-0017.explanation: Correct: B. Tanvir is recalling a specific personal event from a particular time and place, which is episodic memory.

distractor_notes.A: Semantic memory is general knowledge and facts, not a personal event.
distractor_notes.C: Procedural memory is for skills and how to do things.
distractor_notes.D: Prospective memory is remembering to do something in the future.

dq-0018.question: Lucia has not ridden a bicycle in ten years. She climbs onto one and rides smoothly without thinking about each step, but she cannot explain in words how she keeps her balance. Which of the following types of memory best explains her ability?
dq-0018.explanation: Correct: A. Lucia's skill is stored as an implicit memory for a procedure, which is hard to explain in words.

distractor_notes.B: Episodic memory is for personal events, which can be described.
distractor_notes.C: Semantic memory is for facts and general knowledge, which can be described.
distractor_notes.D: Prospective memory is about remembering future actions.

dq-0019.question: Before leaving school, Jamal tells himself he needs to stop at the pharmacy on his way home. That afternoon, he remembers and picks up his sister's medicine. Which of the following types of memory did Jamal use?
dq-0019.explanation: Correct: D. Remembering to carry out an action in the future is prospective memory.

distractor_notes.A: Episodic memory is recalling a past personal event.
distractor_notes.B: Semantic memory is recalling general facts.
distractor_notes.C: Procedural memory is for skills such as riding a bicycle.

dq-0020.question: While solving a math problem in her head, Mei silently repeats the numbers 47 and 38 to herself so she can keep them in mind. According to the working memory model, which of the following components is Mei mainly using?
dq-0020.explanation: Correct: C. The phonological loop holds sounds and words, such as numbers repeated silently.

distractor_notes.A: The central executive directs attention and coordinates the other components.
distractor_notes.B: The visuospatial sketchpad holds images and spatial information.
distractor_notes.D: Echoic memory is brief sensory memory for sound in the multi-store model, not a working memory component.

dq-0021.question: Dr. Park asks students to study a word list by deciding whether each word fits into the sentence "The ___ was on the table." According to the levels of processing model, which of the following types of encoding are the students using?
dq-0021.explanation: Correct: A. Judging whether a word fits a sentence depends on its meaning, which is semantic encoding, the deepest level of processing.

distractor_notes.B: Structural encoding focuses on how words look, the shallowest level.
distractor_notes.C: Phonemic encoding focuses on how words sound.
distractor_notes.D: Iconic memory is brief visual sensory memory, not a level of processing.

dq-0022.question: A psychologist gives the same intelligence test to 200 students in September and again to the same students in October. Each student's score is very similar on both days. Which of the following best describes the test?
dq-0022.explanation: Correct: C. Getting similar results when the test is given twice shows test-retest reliability.

distractor_notes.A: Validity is whether a test measures what it is meant to measure, which these scores do not show.
distractor_notes.B: Standardization is about using consistent procedures, not about consistent scores.
distractor_notes.D: Nothing in the stem suggests unfair results for any group.

dq-0023.question: A company creates a test to predict how well applicants will perform as sales representatives. Applicants' scores on the test strongly match their supervisors' performance ratings one year later. Which of the following is this an example of?
dq-0023.explanation: Correct: A. The test scores accurately forecast a later outcome, which is predictive validity.

distractor_notes.B: Test-retest reliability compares scores from two administrations of the same test.
distractor_notes.C: Split-half reliability compares scores on two halves of one test.
distractor_notes.D: Standardization is about consistent testing procedures.

dq-0024.question: Every student taking a state aptitude test receives the same directions, has the same time limit, and sits in a quiet room. Which of the following psychometric principles does this best illustrate?
dq-0024.explanation: Correct: D. Giving the test with consistent procedures and in consistent settings is standardization.

distractor_notes.A: Construct validity asks whether a test measures the trait it claims to measure.
distractor_notes.B: Test-retest reliability compares scores across two testing times.
distractor_notes.C: Predictive validity is how well scores forecast a future outcome.

dq-0025.question: Early intelligence tests divided mental age by chronological age and multiplied by 100. A 12-year-old child performs at the level of a typical 10-year-old. Which of the following is closest to this child's IQ on the early formula?
dq-0025.explanation: Correct: B. Mental age 10 divided by chronological age 12, times 100, is about 83.

distractor_notes.A: 22 comes from adding the two ages instead of dividing.
distractor_notes.C: 100 would mean mental age equals chronological age, which is not the case here.
distractor_notes.D: 120 comes from dividing 12 by 10, which reverses the formula.

dq-0026.question: Dr. Alvarez finds that students who score high on a vocabulary test usually also score high on tests of math, spatial reasoning, and memory. She concludes that one underlying ability influences performance on all of these tasks. Which of the following does her conclusion best support?
dq-0026.explanation: Correct: C. A single factor behind performance on many different tasks is the idea of general intelligence, or g.

distractor_notes.A: Multiple intelligences proposes separate, independent abilities.
distractor_notes.B: Emotional intelligence is about perceiving and managing emotions.
distractor_notes.D: Mental age is part of an early IQ formula, not a theory of structure.

dq-0027.question: To remember the phone number 5558675309, Rosa mentally splits it into three smaller sets: 555, 867, and 5309. Which of the following best describes the strategy Rosa is using?
dq-0027.explanation: Correct: D. Combining digits into a few meaningful units is chunking, which makes the number easier to hold and encode.

distractor_notes.A: The method of loci links items to places along a familiar route.
distractor_notes.B: The serial position effect is about memory for items by their place in a list.
distractor_notes.C: The spacing effect is about spreading study over time.

dq-0028.question: Before giving a speech, Amara imagines placing each of her main points at a different spot along the path through her house. During the speech she mentally walks the path to recall each point in order. Which of the following best describes her strategy?
dq-0028.explanation: Correct: A. Linking each item to a location on a familiar route is the method of loci, a mnemonic device.

distractor_notes.B: Chunking groups information into meaningful units.
distractor_notes.C: Maintenance rehearsal is repeating information over and over.
distractor_notes.D: The primacy effect is better memory for items at the start of a list.

dq-0029.question: Dr. Lindgren has two groups study the same vocabulary words. Group 1 studies for four hours the night before a test. Group 2 studies for one hour each day over four days. A week later, Group 2 scores higher. Which of the following best explains the result?
dq-0029.explanation: Correct: C. Study spread over time, rather than crammed at once, leads to better long-term memory, which is the spacing effect.

distractor_notes.A: The primacy effect concerns items at the start of a list, not how study time is arranged.
distractor_notes.B: Chunking is grouping information, which neither group is described as doing.
distractor_notes.D: Context-dependent memory depends on matching the setting at study and test.

dq-0030.question: After a head injury, Mr. Osei can describe his childhood and his wedding in detail. He cannot form new memories, so each morning he meets his nurse as if for the first time. Which of the following best describes his condition?
dq-0030.explanation: Correct: B. Being unable to form new memories after an injury is anterograde amnesia.

distractor_notes.A: Retrograde amnesia is losing memories formed before an injury, which Mr. Osei has kept.
distractor_notes.C: Infantile amnesia is the normal lack of memories from early childhood.
distractor_notes.D: Source amnesia is forgetting where a memory came from.

dq-0031.question: Dr. Kim asks one group of students to repeat the definition of a term over and over. She asks a second group to connect the term to events in their own lives. A week later, the second group remembers much more. Which of the following best explains the difference?
dq-0031.explanation: Correct: B. Linking material to personal meaning is elaborative rehearsal, which supports retention better than simple repetition.

distractor_notes.A: Maintenance rehearsal is the simple repetition that the first group used.
distractor_notes.C: Chunking is grouping items into larger units.
distractor_notes.D: Iconic memory is a brief visual sensory memory lasting a fraction of a second.

dq-0032.question: Dr. Singh's family says she walked, talked, and attended a birthday party before she turned two. As an adult, she cannot recall any of these events or anything else from before about age three. Which of the following best explains this?
dq-0032.explanation: Correct: D. Adults typically cannot recall events from the earliest years of life, which is infantile amnesia.

distractor_notes.A: Retrograde amnesia follows an injury or illness and erases memories formed earlier.
distractor_notes.B: Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories.
distractor_notes.C: Nothing suggests a disease; this pattern is typical of adults.

dq-0033.question: On a short-answer quiz, Kofi writes the names of the five Great Lakes without any hints or answer choices. Which of the following retrieval processes is Kofi using?
dq-0033.explanation: Correct: A. Remembering information without cues is recall.

distractor_notes.B: Recognition identifies information when cues, such as answer choices, are provided.
distractor_notes.C: Rehearsal is repeating information to keep it in memory.
distractor_notes.D: Consolidation is the process that stabilizes a memory after it forms.

dq-0034.question: Students who studied for a test in the same classroom where they take it earn higher scores than students who studied in the library. Which of the following best explains this finding?
dq-0034.explanation: Correct: C. Retrieval improves when the environment matches the setting where the information was encoded.

distractor_notes.A: Mood-congruent memory favors memories that match the person's current mood.
distractor_notes.B: State-dependent memory depends on a matching physical state, such as alertness.
distractor_notes.D: The testing effect is better memory from practicing retrieval.

dq-0035.question: Dr. Haddad has half of her students re-read a chapter and the other half take a practice quiz on the same chapter. A week later, the practice-quiz group scores higher on a final test. Which of the following best explains the result?
dq-0035.explanation: Correct: A. Practicing retrieval, as quizzing does, strengthens memory more than re-reading, which is the testing effect.

distractor_notes.B: The serial position effect is about where an item falls in a list.
distractor_notes.C: The misinformation effect is memory distorted by misleading information.
distractor_notes.D: Source amnesia is forgetting where information was learned.

dq-0036.question: Ivy gets a new locker combination at the start of the semester, but for weeks she keeps entering her old combination by mistake. Which of the following best explains her difficulty?
dq-0036.explanation: Correct: C. Older learning gets in the way of recalling new information, which is proactive interference.

distractor_notes.A: Retroactive interference is new learning disrupting memory of old information, the reverse of this case.
distractor_notes.B: Encoding failure means information never entered memory; Ivy did learn the new number.
distractor_notes.D: Repression is forgetting to protect the ego from distress.

dq-0037.question: Participants watch a video of a car accident. Some are asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" into each other, and others are asked about the cars that "hit" each other. A week later, the "smashed" group is more likely to report seeing broken glass that was not in the video. Which of the following best explains this result?
dq-0037.explanation: Correct: D. The wording of the question introduced misleading information that changed what participants remembered.

distractor_notes.A: Source amnesia is forgetting where a memory came from.
distractor_notes.B: Imagination inflation is greater confidence in a memory after imagining the event.
distractor_notes.C: The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon is failing to retrieve a word that feels familiar.

dq-0038.question: A researcher tests how many items from a list of nonsense syllables people remember at several times after learning. The graph shows that most forgetting happens soon after learning, and then the rate of forgetting slows. Which of the following does this pattern illustrate?
dq-0038.explanation: Correct: B. Rapid early loss that levels off over time is the forgetting curve.

distractor_notes.A: The spacing effect is about distributing study sessions.
distractor_notes.C: The primacy effect is better memory for early items in a list.
distractor_notes.D: Retroactive interference is new learning disrupting old memories.

dq-0039.question: Why did Dr. Mbeki randomly assign students to the two groups?
options: To make the groups likely to be similar at the start
To make sure every student studied the same number of words
To allow the results to apply to all college students
To keep students from learning which group they were in
dq-0039.explanation: Correct: A. Random assignment spreads participant differences evenly across groups, so differences in recall are more likely due to the study schedule.

distractor_notes.B: Giving everyone the same word list is a control, not random assignment.
distractor_notes.C: Applying results to a population depends on random sampling, not random assignment.
distractor_notes.D: Random assignment does not hide group membership; that would be blinding.

dq-0040.question: According to the graph, how many more words did the distributed group recall than the massed group 14 days after study?
dq-0040.explanation: Correct: C. At 14 days the distributed group recalled 16 words and the massed group recalled 8, a difference of 8.

distractor_notes.A: 2 is the difference at 1 day, not 14 days.
distractor_notes.B: 7 is the difference at 7 days, not 14 days.
distractor_notes.D: 16 is the distributed group's mean, not the difference.

dq-0041.question: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the results?
options: Both groups recalled more words as more days passed.
The distributed group recalled more words at every test time.
The massed group forgot words more slowly than the distributed group.
Every student should study in three short sessions.
dq-0041.explanation: Correct: B. The distributed group's mean was higher than the massed group's at 1, 7, and 14 days.

distractor_notes.A: Recall for both groups fell over time.
distractor_notes.C: The massed group's recall dropped faster, so it forgot more quickly.
distractor_notes.D: The study cannot show what is best for every student.

dq-0042.question: Dr. Perez randomly assigns 80 students to drink either a caffeinated or a decaffeinated beverage before studying a word list. A day later, he tests how many words each student remembers. Which of the following research methods is Dr. Perez using?
dq-0042.explanation: Correct: A. Dr. Perez manipulates the beverage and randomly assigns students, which defines an experiment.

distractor_notes.B: A correlational study measures variables without manipulating them.
distractor_notes.C: A case study is an in-depth examination of one individual or a small group.
distractor_notes.D: Naturalistic observation records behavior in its natural setting without intervening.

dq-0043.question: A researcher surveys 300 high school students about their nightly hours of sleep and collects their grade point averages (GPAs). She finds a correlation of +0.45 between sleep and GPA. Which of the following is the best conclusion from this result?
options: Sleep and GPA have no relationship in this sample
Getting more sleep causes students' GPAs to rise
Earning a high GPA causes students to sleep more
Students who sleep more tend to have higher GPAs
dq-0043.explanation: Correct: D. A positive correlation means the two variables tend to rise together, but it does not show cause.

distractor_notes.A: A correlation of +0.45 indicates a moderate positive relationship, not none.
distractor_notes.B: Correlation cannot show that sleep causes higher GPAs.
distractor_notes.C: Correlation cannot show the direction of cause either.

dq-0044.question: Five participants recalled the following numbers of words from a list: 8, 10, 10, 12, 20. What is the mean number of words recalled?
dq-0044.explanation: Correct: C. The sum is 60, and 60 divided by 5 participants equals 12.

distractor_notes.A: 8 is the lowest score.
distractor_notes.B: 10 is the median and the mode, not the mean.
distractor_notes.D: 20 is the highest score.

dq-0045.question: What is the dependent variable in this study?
options: Whether students talked on a phone while walking
The number of students in each group
The campus square where the walk took place
dq-0045.explanation: Correct: B. The researcher measured whether each student noticed the clown, which is the outcome and so the dependent variable.

distractor_notes.A: Phone use is what the researcher manipulated, the independent variable.
distractor_notes.C: The number of students per group was held equal, so it is not measured as an outcome.
distractor_notes.D: The setting was the same for everyone; it is a constant, not a variable.

dq-0046.question: What percentage of the phone group noticed the clown?
dq-0046.explanation: Correct: A. 25 of the 100 students in the phone group noticed the clown, which is 25%.

distractor_notes.B: 40% is the percentage of the no-phone group that did not notice.
distractor_notes.C: 60% is the percentage of the no-phone group that noticed.
distractor_notes.D: 75% is the percentage of the phone group that did not notice.

dq-0047.question: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the results?
options: Most students in both groups noticed the clown.
Students who noticed the clown were more likely to be on a phone.
Phone use harms attention in every person.
Talking on a phone reduced how many students noticed the clown.
dq-0047.explanation: Correct: D. Students were randomly assigned, and fewer in the phone group noticed the clown, so phone use likely reduced noticing.

distractor_notes.A: Only 25 of 100 in the phone group noticed, so not most students in both groups.
distractor_notes.B: This reverses the pattern; the no-phone group noticed more often.
distractor_notes.C: The study cannot show an effect on every person.

dq-0048.question: Dr. Huang tells participants they will complete a puzzle task. The puzzle is actually impossible, and she is measuring how people respond to failure. When the session ends, she explains the real purpose of the study and answers participants' questions. Which of the following ethical procedures does this best illustrate?
dq-0048.explanation: Correct: C. Explaining the true purpose and answering questions after the study is debriefing.

distractor_notes.A: Informed consent happens before the study and explains what participation involves.
distractor_notes.B: Confidentiality is keeping participants' data private.
distractor_notes.D: Protection from harm is limiting risk to participants during the study.

dq-0049.question: Dr. Silva wants to study whether sleep improves memory. In her study, she defines memory as the number of words a participant correctly recalls from a 20-word list ten minutes after studying. Which of the following research design elements does this definition best illustrate?
dq-0049.explanation: Correct: B. An operational definition states exactly how a variable will be measured, here memory as words recalled.

distractor_notes.A: Random sampling is selecting participants from a population by chance.
distractor_notes.C: A confounding variable is an uncontrolled factor that could affect the outcome.
distractor_notes.D: A placebo is an inactive treatment given to a control group.

dq-0050.question: Five students solved a puzzle in the following numbers of minutes: 4, 9, 12, 15, 17. What is the range of these times?
dq-0050.explanation: Correct: D. The range is the highest value minus the lowest, 17 minus 4, which is 13.

distractor_notes.A: 4 is the lowest time, not the range.
distractor_notes.B: 11 is about the mean, not the range.
distractor_notes.C: 12 is the median, not the range.

dq-0051.question: Leila watches a 3D movie wearing special glasses. Each of her eyes receives a slightly different image of the scene, and the film appears to have depth. Which of the following depth cues best explains this experience?
dq-0051.explanation: Correct: C. The brain uses the difference between the two eyes' images to judge distance, which is retinal disparity.

distractor_notes.A: Convergence is the inward turning of the eyes for near objects, not a difference between images.
distractor_notes.B: Relative size is a monocular cue and works with one eye.
distractor_notes.D: Interposition is a monocular cue in which one object blocks another.

dq-0052.question: Dr. Bello shows two groups the same ambiguous drawing that can look like either a rabbit or a duck. Before seeing it, one group looks at pictures of rabbits and the other looks at pictures of ducks. Most people in each group see the animal they were just shown. Which of the following best explains the difference?
dq-0052.explanation: Correct: A. Prior experience created a readiness to perceive the drawing in a particular way, which is a perceptual set.

distractor_notes.B: Closure is filling in gaps to see a complete form.
distractor_notes.C: Apparent movement is seeing motion in still images.
distractor_notes.D: Retinal disparity is a binocular depth cue.

dq-0053.question: The lights on a theater sign turn on one after another in a row, a fraction of a second apart. Viewers say they see a single light moving along the sign. Which of the following best explains what viewers perceive?
dq-0053.explanation: Correct: D. Perceiving motion from stationary stimuli shown in quick succession is apparent movement.

distractor_notes.A: Texture gradient is a depth cue based on changes in texture.
distractor_notes.B: Size constancy keeps an object's size stable as distance changes.
distractor_notes.C: Convergence is a binocular depth cue.

dq-0054.question: Meera meets a quiet man who wears glasses and loves books. She decides he is more likely a librarian than a salesperson, even though there are many more salespeople than librarians. Which of the following best explains her judgment?
dq-0054.explanation: Correct: B. She judged by how well the man matches her image of a librarian and ignored how common each job is.

distractor_notes.A: Availability depends on how easily examples come to mind, not on a match to a stereotype.
distractor_notes.C: Framing is about the wording of options.
distractor_notes.D: Functional fixedness is seeing objects only in their usual use.

dq-0055.question: A fair coin lands on heads five times in a row. Dr. Reyes's friend bets a large sum that the next flip will be tails because tails is "due." Which of the following is the best description of the friend's reasoning?
dq-0055.explanation: Correct: C. Believing past random events change the odds of the next one is the gambler's fallacy.

distractor_notes.A: The sunk-cost fallacy is about continuing because of past investment.
distractor_notes.B: A mental set is repeating a past strategy.
distractor_notes.D: Priming is an earlier cue influencing a later response.

dq-0056.question: A student solves several math problems using the same three-step method. When a new problem has a much simpler solution, she still uses the three-step method and takes much longer. Which of the following best describes her thinking?
dq-0056.explanation: Correct: A. Sticking with a strategy that worked before, even when a better one exists, is a mental set.

distractor_notes.B: Functional fixedness is limited to seeing objects only in their usual use.
distractor_notes.C: Divergent thinking produces many different ideas, which she does not.
distractor_notes.D: Framing is about how wording changes a choice.

dq-0057.question: In the model shown, which numbered arrow represents encoding information into long-term memory?
dq-0057.explanation: Correct: B. Arrow 2 carries information from short-term memory into long-term memory, which is encoding.

distractor_notes.A: Arrow 1 moves information from sensory memory into short-term memory.
distractor_notes.C: Arrow 3 moves information from long-term memory back into short-term memory, which is retrieval.
distractor_notes.D: Arrow 4 keeps information within short-term memory.

dq-0058.question: A test developer compares each student's scores on the odd-numbered items of a test with the same student's scores on the even-numbered items. The two sets of scores are very similar. Which of the following does this result best support?
dq-0058.explanation: Correct: D. Consistent scores across two halves of the same test support split-half reliability.

distractor_notes.A: Test-retest reliability compares scores from two separate testing times.
distractor_notes.B: Construct validity is whether the test measures the intended trait.
distractor_notes.C: Predictive validity is how well scores forecast a future outcome.

dq-0059.question: After hearing a list of 15 unrelated words read aloud, participants recall the last few words on the list most easily. Which of the following best explains this result?
dq-0059.explanation: Correct: B. Items at the end of a list are still active in memory when recall begins, which is the recency effect.

distractor_notes.A: The primacy effect is better memory for the first items.
distractor_notes.C: The spacing effect is about distributing study over time.
distractor_notes.D: Chunking is grouping items into larger units.

dq-0060.question: Dev studies for six hours straight the night before his exam. He does well the next morning but remembers very little of the material a month later. Which of the following best describes Dev's study method?
dq-0060.explanation: Correct: A. Studying all at once in one long session is massed practice, which usually produces weaker long-term memory.

distractor_notes.B: Distributed practice spreads study over several sessions.
distractor_notes.C: Elaborative rehearsal links information to meaning; no linking is described.
distractor_notes.D: The primacy effect depends on position in a list.

dq-0061.question: A waiter takes a 12-item order from a large table without writing it down. When he recalls it, he remembers the first few items best because he had time to repeat them before more items arrived. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
dq-0061.explanation: Correct: C. Early items in a list get more rehearsal and are remembered better, which is the primacy effect.

distractor_notes.A: The recency effect is better memory for the last items.
distractor_notes.B: The method of loci links items to places.
distractor_notes.D: Massed practice is studying all at once.

dq-0062.question: In the model shown, which of the following does Arrow 4 best represent?
dq-0062.explanation: Correct: D. Arrow 4 returns to short-term memory, which shows repeating information to keep it active, or maintenance rehearsal.

distractor_notes.A: Elaborative rehearsal links information to meaning and supports movement into long-term memory.
distractor_notes.B: Echoic memory is a sensory store for sounds.
distractor_notes.C: Consolidation stabilizes memory in long-term storage.

dq-0063.question: After a car accident, Mr. Dubois cannot remember the three years before the crash. He learns new information normally since the accident. Which of the following best describes his condition?
dq-0063.explanation: Correct: B. Losing memories formed before an injury is retrograde amnesia.

distractor_notes.A: Anterograde amnesia is trouble forming new memories, which he does not have.
distractor_notes.C: Infantile amnesia is the normal lack of early childhood memories.
distractor_notes.D: Nothing in the stem suggests a progressive disease.

dq-0064.question: A researcher flashes a grid of 12 letters on a screen for one-twentieth of a second. Participants report seeing all the letters, but within a second they can name only a few. Which of the following best explains this result?
dq-0064.explanation: Correct: C. A brief visual memory that fades within a fraction of a second is iconic memory.

distractor_notes.A: Echoic memory holds sounds, not images.
distractor_notes.B: Procedural memory is for skills.
distractor_notes.D: Prospective memory is for future tasks.

dq-0065.question: Ravi feels sad after a bad day. He finds it much easier to remember sad events from his past than happy ones. Which of the following best explains his recall?
dq-0065.explanation: Correct: A. Memories that match a person's current mood are easier to retrieve, which is mood-congruent memory.

distractor_notes.B: State-dependent memory depends on a matching physical state.
distractor_notes.C: Context-dependent memory depends on a matching environment.
distractor_notes.D: The testing effect is better memory after retrieval practice.

dq-0066.question: A student studies for a test while having a strong cup of coffee. She finds that she recalls the material better if she drinks a cup of coffee again before the test. Which of the following best explains her experience?
dq-0066.explanation: Correct: D. Retrieval improves when the physical state matches the state during encoding, which is state-dependent memory.

distractor_notes.A: Context-dependent memory depends on a matching place, not the body's state.
distractor_notes.B: Mood-congruent memory depends on a matching emotion.
distractor_notes.C: The testing effect is about practicing retrieval.

dq-0067.question: Before a test, Alana quizzes herself on each chapter. She realizes she knows chapter 3 well but not chapter 5, so she spends more time on chapter 5. Which of the following best describes Alana's awareness of what she knows?
dq-0067.explanation: Correct: B. Thinking about and judging your own knowledge is metacognition, which helps guide study.

distractor_notes.A: Recall is retrieving information without cues, not judging what you know.
distractor_notes.C: Chunking is grouping information.
distractor_notes.D: The primacy effect depends on list position.

dq-0068.question: Omar learns Spanish vocabulary this semester. He now has trouble remembering the French words he learned last year. Which of the following best explains his difficulty?
dq-0068.explanation: Correct: C. New learning, Spanish, is getting in the way of recalling older learning, French, which is retroactive interference.

distractor_notes.A: Proactive interference is old learning disrupting new learning, the reverse of this case.
distractor_notes.B: Omar did learn the French words, so they were encoded.
distractor_notes.D: Repression is forgetting to protect the ego from distress.

dq-0069.question: Priya is sure she knows the name of an actor. She remembers the name starts with M and has two syllables, but she cannot say it. Which of the following best describes her experience?
dq-0069.explanation: Correct: D. Knowing a word is in memory but failing to retrieve it fully is the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon.

distractor_notes.A: Source amnesia is forgetting where information came from.
distractor_notes.B: Priya clearly encoded part of the name.
distractor_notes.C: Imagination inflation is greater confidence after imagining an event.

dq-0070.question: Dr. Fischer, a psychodynamic theorist, suggests that an adult cannot remember a painful childhood event because the mind pushed it out of awareness to protect itself from distress. Which of the following concepts does Dr. Fischer's explanation describe?
dq-0070.explanation: Correct: A. Psychodynamic theorists propose that painful memories are pushed out of awareness to defend the ego, which is repression.

distractor_notes.B: Encoding failure means the event never entered memory.
distractor_notes.C: Proactive interference is old learning disrupting new learning.
distractor_notes.D: The misinformation effect is memory distorted by misleading information.

dq-0071.question: Dr. Mehta concludes that a child's musical ability reflects both the traits the child was born with and the lessons and practice the child has received. Which of the following best describes this conclusion?
dq-0071.explanation: Correct: B. The conclusion gives weight to both inherited traits and experience, which is the interaction of nature and nurture.

distractor_notes.A: Nature only would ignore the lessons and practice.
distractor_notes.C: Nurture only would ignore inborn traits.
distractor_notes.D: Natural selection explains how traits spread across generations, not one child's ability.

dq-0072.question: Dr. Chen compares the personality scores of pairs of siblings who were born at the same time and are genetically identical with the scores of pairs who are not genetically identical. Which of the following research methods is Dr. Chen using?
dq-0072.explanation: Correct: D. Comparing pairs who share the same genes with pairs who do not is the logic of a twin study.

distractor_notes.A: An adoption study compares children with their birth and adoptive families.
distractor_notes.B: A family study compares relatives with different degrees of genetic relatedness, not same-age siblings.
distractor_notes.C: A case study examines one individual or group in depth.

dq-0073.question: A researcher compares the intelligence scores of children with the scores of the parents who raised them and with the scores of their birth parents, whom the children never met. Which of the following research methods is the researcher using?
dq-0073.explanation: Correct: C. Separating the effects of birth parents' genes from the home environment is the purpose of an adoption study.

distractor_notes.A: A twin study compares pairs of twins.
distractor_notes.B: A family study compares biological relatives who usually live together.
distractor_notes.D: Naturalistic observation records behavior in natural settings without intervening.

dq-0074.question: Dr. Osei argues that infants smile at caregivers because this behavior helped the ancestors of today's infants get care and survive. Which of the following psychological perspectives best matches this argument?
dq-0074.explanation: Correct: A. Explaining a behavior by how it improved survival and reproductive success reflects the evolutionary perspective.

distractor_notes.B: The behavioral perspective focuses on learning from the environment.
distractor_notes.C: The humanistic perspective focuses on growth and personal choice.
distractor_notes.D: The sociocultural perspective focuses on culture and social context.

dq-0075.question: In the early twentieth century, some people used ideas about inherited traits to support laws that kept certain groups of people from having children. Which of the following terms describes this discriminatory misuse of the evolutionary perspective?
dq-0075.explanation: Correct: D. Applying ideas about heredity to discriminate against groups is eugenics.

distractor_notes.A: Natural selection is a process in nature, not a set of laws.
distractor_notes.B: Behavioral genetics studies how genes and environment affect behavior; it is not a discriminatory movement.
distractor_notes.C: Environmental influence refers to external experiences.

dq-0076.question: Two children have similar inherited traits. One attends an enriched preschool and the other does not. At age six, the first child scores much higher on a reading test. Which of the following best explains the difference in scores?
dq-0076.explanation: Correct: B. The children differ in their experiences, so the preschool environment is the best explanation.

distractor_notes.A: The children are said to have similar inherited traits.
distractor_notes.C: Natural selection does not explain differences between two individuals.
distractor_notes.D: The children's genetic similarity cannot explain a difference in scores.

dq-0077.question: Which of the following parts of the nervous system consists of the brain and the spinal cord?
dq-0077.explanation: Correct: A. The brain and spinal cord together make up the central nervous system.

distractor_notes.B: The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord.
distractor_notes.C: The autonomic nervous system is part of the peripheral system.
distractor_notes.D: The somatic nervous system is also part of the peripheral system.

dq-0078.question: While walking alone at night, Sam hears footsteps behind him. His heart pounds, his pupils widen, and his breathing speeds up. Which of the following nervous system divisions is mainly responsible?
dq-0078.explanation: Correct: C. The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for action when a threat appears.

distractor_notes.A: The somatic system controls voluntary muscle movement.
distractor_notes.B: The parasympathetic system calms the body after arousal.
distractor_notes.D: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord, not the division that produces this response.

dq-0079.question: After a large meal, Dr. Grant sits down and relaxes. Her heart rate slows and her body digests the food. Which of the following nervous system divisions is mainly responsible for these changes?
dq-0079.explanation: Correct: D. The parasympathetic nervous system calms the body and supports digestion.

distractor_notes.A: The somatic system controls voluntary movement.
distractor_notes.B: The sympathetic system speeds up the body in response to threat.
distractor_notes.C: The central nervous system is not a division of the autonomic system.

dq-0080.question: Aisha chooses to pick up a pen from her desk. Which of the following parts of the nervous system sends the signals from her brain to the muscles of her hand?
dq-0080.explanation: Correct: B. Voluntary movement of skeletal muscles is controlled by the somatic nervous system.

distractor_notes.A: The autonomic system controls involuntary processes.
distractor_notes.C: The parasympathetic system is a branch of the autonomic system.
distractor_notes.D: The sympathetic system is a branch of the autonomic system.

dq-0081.question: Without thinking about it, a person's heart keeps beating and food keeps moving through the digestive system. Which of the following systems governs these involuntary processes?
dq-0081.explanation: Correct: A. Involuntary processes such as heartbeat and digestion are governed by the autonomic nervous system.

distractor_notes.B: The somatic system governs voluntary movement.
distractor_notes.C: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord.
distractor_notes.D: The endocrine system uses hormones and is not part of the nervous system.

dq-0082.question: Dr. Ito's patient has damaged the nerves that connect the spinal cord to the muscles in the patient's hand. The patient's brain and spinal cord are not injured. Which of the following parts of the nervous system is damaged?
dq-0082.explanation: Correct: D. Nerves outside the brain and spinal cord belong to the peripheral nervous system.

distractor_notes.A: The central nervous system is not injured.
distractor_notes.B: The brain is not injured.
distractor_notes.C: The spinal cord is not injured.

dq-0083.question: Marcus touches a hot stove and pulls his hand away before he feels any pain. Which of the following types of neurons carries the message from the spinal cord to the muscles in his arm?
dq-0083.explanation: Correct: C. Motor neurons carry commands from the spinal cord to muscles, producing the movement.

distractor_notes.A: Sensory neurons carry the message from the hand to the spinal cord.
distractor_notes.B: Glial cells support neurons but do not carry the message.
distractor_notes.D: Interneurons connect sensory and motor neurons inside the spinal cord.

dq-0084.question: A stimulus that is too weak to affect a neuron produces no response. Once a stimulus is strong enough, the neuron fires with the same strength no matter how much stronger the stimulus gets. Which of the following principles does this describe?
dq-0084.explanation: Correct: B. A neuron either fires completely or not at all, which is the all-or-none principle.

distractor_notes.A: The refractory period is the brief time after firing when a neuron cannot fire.
distractor_notes.C: Reuptake is the reabsorption of neurotransmitters.
distractor_notes.D: Resting potential is the neuron's state when it is not firing.

dq-0085.question: Immediately after a neuron fires, it cannot fire again for a brief time, even if it receives a very strong stimulus. Which of the following terms describes this brief time?
dq-0085.explanation: Correct: C. The brief period when a neuron cannot fire again is the refractory period.

distractor_notes.A: Resting potential is the neuron's state before firing.
distractor_notes.B: Threshold is the level of stimulation needed to fire.
distractor_notes.D: Reuptake is the reabsorption of neurotransmitters by the sending neuron.

dq-0086.question: A medication that increases GABA activity makes many people feel calmer and less anxious. Which of the following best explains why this happens?
options: GABA makes neurons less likely to fire.
GABA makes neurons more likely to fire.
GABA triggers the release of adrenaline.
GABA blocks the reuptake of dopamine.
dq-0086.explanation: Correct: A. GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter, so more GABA activity lowers neural firing and brings calm.

distractor_notes.B: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter, not an excitatory one.
distractor_notes.C: GABA does not trigger adrenaline release.
distractor_notes.D: GABA does not act as a reuptake inhibitor for dopamine.

dq-0087.question: A neurotransmitter released at the junction between motor neurons and muscles causes the muscles to contract. A disruption of this chemical's action can cause muscle weakness. Which of the following neurotransmitters is described?
dq-0087.explanation: Correct: B. Acetylcholine triggers muscle contraction at the neuromuscular junction.

distractor_notes.A: Dopamine is linked to reward and movement control in the brain.
distractor_notes.C: Serotonin is linked to mood, sleep, and appetite.
distractor_notes.D: Endorphins reduce pain.

dq-0088.question: After a long run, a marathon runner feels less pain and a sense of well-being. A researcher says this effect comes from the body's own pain-relieving chemicals. Which of the following neurotransmitters best fits this description?
dq-0088.explanation: Correct: D. Endorphins are natural pain relievers released during intense exercise.

distractor_notes.A: Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter, linked to learning and memory.
distractor_notes.B: Substance P helps transmit pain signals.
distractor_notes.C: Norepinephrine is linked to alertness and arousal.

dq-0089.question: Dr. Yilmaz finds that the level of a particular hormone rises at night and signals the body to prepare for sleep. Which of the following hormones is described?
dq-0089.explanation: Correct: C. Melatonin rises in the evening and helps regulate the sleep cycle.

distractor_notes.A: Leptin signals fullness.
distractor_notes.B: Ghrelin signals hunger.
distractor_notes.D: Oxytocin is linked to bonding and trust.

dq-0090.question: A drug blocks the sending neuron from reabsorbing serotonin. As a result, more serotonin stays in the synapse. Which of the following best describes this drug?
dq-0090.explanation: Correct: A. Blocking reabsorption of a neurotransmitter is the action of a reuptake inhibitor.

distractor_notes.B: An agonist mimics or increases a neurotransmitter's effect.
distractor_notes.C: An antagonist blocks a neurotransmitter's effect.
distractor_notes.D: A depressant is a category of drugs that slows neural activity.

dq-0091.question: Dr. Haas studies cells in the brain that wrap around neurons to insulate them, provide structure, and carry away waste, but that do not themselves transmit information. Which of the following types of cells is Dr. Haas studying?
dq-0091.explanation: Correct: B. Cells that support, insulate, and clean up around neurons without transmitting information are glial cells.

distractor_notes.A: Sensory neurons do transmit information, from the senses to the central nervous system.
distractor_notes.C: Motor neurons transmit commands to muscles.
distractor_notes.D: Interneurons transmit messages between other neurons.

dq-0092.question: After drinking several cups of strong coffee, Jun feels very alert and notices that his heart is beating faster. Which of the following categories of psychoactive drugs does caffeine belong to?
dq-0092.explanation: Correct: D. Caffeine increases neural activity, which defines a stimulant.

distractor_notes.A: Depressants slow neural activity.
distractor_notes.B: Hallucinogens distort perception or thinking.
distractor_notes.C: Opioids act as pain relievers.

dq-0093.question: Over several months, Rosa needs larger and larger doses of a drug to get the same effect she first felt from a small dose. Which of the following terms describes this change?
dq-0093.explanation: Correct: A. Needing more of a drug to get the same effect is tolerance.

distractor_notes.B: Withdrawal is the set of symptoms after stopping a drug.
distractor_notes.C: Reuptake is the reabsorption of a neurotransmitter.
distractor_notes.D: Depolarization is a change in a neuron's electrical charge.

dq-0094.question: A researcher finds that people's brains release a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of reward and motivation when they eat a favorite food or win a game. Which of the following neurotransmitters best fits this description?
dq-0094.explanation: Correct: C. Dopamine is associated with reward, pleasure, and motivation.

distractor_notes.A: GABA is inhibitory and linked to calming.
distractor_notes.B: Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter.
distractor_notes.D: Substance P helps transmit pain signals.

dq-0095.question: After a stroke damages his frontal and temporal lobes, Mr. Perez can no longer speak or understand words. His breathing and heart rate remain steady. Which of the following brain structures continues to control these basic functions?
dq-0095.explanation: Correct: D. The brain stem, including the medulla, controls basic life functions such as breathing and heart rate.

distractor_notes.A: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.
distractor_notes.B: The hippocampus is involved in forming new memories.
distractor_notes.C: The thalamus relays sensory information.

dq-0096.question: After an injury to the lower back of his brain, Mateo staggers when he walks and cannot touch his nose smoothly with his finger. He can think and speak normally. Which of the following brain structures was most likely damaged?
dq-0096.explanation: Correct: A. Poor balance and uncoordinated movement with normal thinking point to the cerebellum.

distractor_notes.B: The amygdala is involved in emotion, especially fear.
distractor_notes.C: The hypothalamus regulates hunger, thirst, and temperature.
distractor_notes.D: The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres.

dq-0097.question: After surgery, a patient remembers his childhood clearly but cannot form new long-term memories. The surgeons removed part of the limbic system. Which of the following structures was most likely removed?
dq-0097.explanation: Correct: B. The hippocampus is needed to form new long-term memories.

distractor_notes.A: The amygdala is involved in emotion, especially fear.
distractor_notes.C: The thalamus relays sensory information.
distractor_notes.D: The hypothalamus regulates hunger, thirst, and temperature.

dq-0098.question: After an accident, a patient no longer shows fear when shown a snake or an angry face, although she can describe these as dangerous. Damage to which of the following limbic system structures is most likely?
dq-0098.explanation: Correct: C. The amygdala is central to fear and other strong emotions.

distractor_notes.A: The thalamus relays sensory information to the cortex.
distractor_notes.B: The hippocampus is involved in forming new memories.
distractor_notes.D: The pituitary gland releases hormones.

dq-0099.question: Dr. Ruiz studies a structure deep in the brain that helps regulate hunger, thirst, and body temperature and controls the pituitary gland. Which of the following structures is Dr. Ruiz studying?
dq-0099.explanation: Correct: A. The hypothalamus regulates basic drives such as hunger and thirst and directs the pituitary gland.

distractor_notes.B: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.
distractor_notes.C: The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres.
distractor_notes.D: The medulla controls breathing and heart rate.

dq-0100.question: After a blow to the back of her head, Kayla's eyes are healthy, but she cannot see objects in part of her visual field. Which of the following lobes of the cortex was most likely damaged?
dq-0100.explanation: Correct: D. Visual information is processed in the occipital lobes at the back of the brain.

distractor_notes.A: The frontal lobe handles planning and movement.
distractor_notes.B: The parietal lobe processes touch and association information.
distractor_notes.C: The temporal lobe handles hearing and language.

dq-0101.question: After damage to the sides of his brain, a patient has trouble recognizing sounds and understanding spoken words. His vision and sense of touch are normal. Which of the following lobes of the cortex was most likely damaged?
dq-0101.explanation: Correct: B. The temporal lobes process auditory and language information.

distractor_notes.A: The occipital lobe processes vision.
distractor_notes.C: The parietal lobe processes touch.
distractor_notes.D: The frontal lobe handles planning and movement.

dq-0102.question: A stroke damages a strip at the rear of the frontal lobe in a patient's left hemisphere. The patient can feel touch normally but cannot move his right arm. Which of the following areas was most likely damaged?
dq-0102.explanation: Correct: C. The motor cortex controls skeletal movement, so damage there can paralyze the opposite arm.

distractor_notes.A: The somatosensory cortex processes touch, which is normal here.
distractor_notes.B: Association areas organize information from several senses.
distractor_notes.D: The prefrontal cortex supports planning and higher-order thinking.

dq-0103.question: A split-brain patient stares at a dot while a word is flashed only to her left visual field. She says she saw nothing, but her left hand picks out the matching object from a group hidden behind a screen. Which of the following best explains the result?
options: The word reached only the left hemisphere, which controls the left hand.
The word was blocked from the visual cortex, so it was never seen.
The surgery damaged the patient's occipital lobes.
The right hemisphere got the word, and speech is usually left-sided.
dq-0103.explanation: Correct: D. Information from the left visual field goes to the right hemisphere, which can guide the left hand but usually cannot produce speech.

distractor_notes.A: The left hemisphere controls the right hand, and it did not receive the word.
distractor_notes.B: The left hand's correct choice shows the word was seen.
distractor_notes.C: Damaged occipital lobes would impair vision for all tasks.

dq-0104.question: After a stroke damages a speech area on one side of a child's brain, she gradually regains much of her speech as other parts of her brain take over the task. Which of the following best explains her recovery?
dq-0104.explanation: Correct: A. The brain's ability to rewire and shift functions to other regions is brain plasticity.

distractor_notes.B: Aphasia is the language impairment, not the recovery.
distractor_notes.C: Lesioning is a research procedure that destroys brain tissue.
distractor_notes.D: Contralateral organization is the opposite-side wiring of the brain.

dq-0105.question: After a stroke, Mr. Adeyemi understands everything said to him but speaks slowly, with great effort, in short phrases. Damage to which of the following areas of the left hemisphere is most likely?
dq-0105.explanation: Correct: B. Broca's area controls speech production, so damage leaves comprehension intact but speech effortful.

distractor_notes.A: Damage to Wernicke's area impairs comprehension, which Mr. Adeyemi has.
distractor_notes.C: The occipital lobe processes vision.
distractor_notes.D: The hippocampus is involved in forming new memories.

dq-0106.question: Dr. Wu wants to see which parts of participants' brains are most active while they solve math problems. She will use images that show changes in blood flow. Which of the following research tools is she using?
dq-0106.explanation: Correct: C. fMRI shows brain activity by detecting changes in blood flow.

distractor_notes.A: EEG records electrical activity with electrodes on the scalp.
distractor_notes.B: Lesioning destroys tissue to see what functions are lost.
distractor_notes.D: A case study examines one individual in depth.

dq-0107.question: A researcher monitors a sleeper whose brain waves look much like those of someone who is awake, even though the sleeper's body is deeply relaxed. The sleeper reports a vivid dream when woken. Which of the following stages is the sleeper most likely in?
dq-0107.explanation: Correct: A. Waking-like brain waves with a relaxed body and vivid dreams describe REM sleep.

distractor_notes.B: Stage 1 has slow, irregular waves as sleep begins.
distractor_notes.C: Stage 2 has sleep spindles and slower waves.
distractor_notes.D: Stage 3 has the slowest waves and is the deepest NREM stage.

dq-0108.question: After flying across several time zones, Amira feels sleepy at midday and wide awake at 3 a.m. for several days. Which of the following best describes this experience?
dq-0108.explanation: Correct: D. Travel across time zones disrupts the circadian rhythm, producing jet lag.

distractor_notes.A: Narcolepsy is sudden sleep attacks, not a time-zone mismatch.
distractor_notes.B: Insomnia is chronic difficulty falling or staying asleep.
distractor_notes.C: REM rebound is extra dreaming sleep after deprivation.

dq-0109.question: During the day, Diego suddenly falls asleep in the middle of conversations and enters dreaming sleep almost immediately. Which of the following sleep disorders best fits this pattern?
dq-0109.explanation: Correct: B. Sudden daytime sleep attacks are the main feature of narcolepsy.

distractor_notes.A: Insomnia is difficulty falling or staying asleep.
distractor_notes.C: Sleep apnea involves repeated pauses in breathing during sleep.
distractor_notes.D: Somnambulism is sleepwalking.

dq-0110.question: Maria snores loudly, and her partner notices that she repeatedly stops breathing for short periods at night. During the day she feels very tired. Which of the following sleep disorders best fits this pattern?
dq-0110.explanation: Correct: C. Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep are the defining feature of sleep apnea.

distractor_notes.A: Insomnia is difficulty falling or staying asleep.
distractor_notes.B: Narcolepsy is sudden sleep attacks.
distractor_notes.D: In this disorder, people physically act out their dreams.

dq-0111.question: For several nights, researchers wake Noah whenever his dreaming sleep begins. When he is finally allowed to sleep undisturbed, he spends much more time than usual in dreaming sleep. Which of the following best describes this result?
dq-0111.explanation: Correct: D. Spending extra time in a sleep stage after being deprived of it is called rebound.

distractor_notes.A: Hypnagogic sensations occur as a person falls asleep.
distractor_notes.B: A circadian rhythm is the roughly 24-hour sleep and wake cycle.
distractor_notes.C: Activation-synthesis is a theory of why people dream.

dq-0112.question: Dr. Lindqvist proposes that dreams are the brain's attempt to make sense of random neural activity during sleep. Which of the following theories does her proposal best match?
dq-0112.explanation: Correct: A. Interpreting random neural firing as a story is the core idea of activation-synthesis theory.

distractor_notes.B: Consolidation theory says dreams relate to organizing memories.
distractor_notes.C: Restoration theory is about why the body needs sleep, not why people dream.
distractor_notes.D: Opponent-process theory explains color vision.

dq-0113.question: Dr. Kapoor plays a tone at many different volumes. At one volume, a participant reports hearing the tone on half of the trials. Which of the following terms describes this volume?
dq-0113.explanation: Correct: B. The lowest intensity detected half of the time is the absolute threshold.

distractor_notes.A: A just-noticeable difference is the smallest change in a stimulus that can be detected.
distractor_notes.C: Sensory adaptation is reduced sensitivity to a constant stimulus.
distractor_notes.D: Transduction is converting stimuli into neural messages.

dq-0114.question: A person holding a 100-gram weight can just notice a difference when 2 grams are added. When holding a 200-gram weight, the person needs 4 grams added to notice a difference. Which of the following principles does this pattern illustrate?
dq-0114.explanation: Correct: D. The needed change grows in proportion to the original stimulus, which is Weber's law.

distractor_notes.A: Absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus that can be detected.
distractor_notes.B: Sensory adaptation is decreased sensitivity to constant stimuli.
distractor_notes.C: Sensory interaction is the way senses influence each other.

dq-0115.question: Soon after walking into a room that smells strongly of perfume, Dana notices the smell less and less. After ten minutes, she hardly notices it at all. Which of the following best explains this change?
dq-0115.explanation: Correct: C. Sensitivity decreases when a stimulus stays constant, which is sensory adaptation.

distractor_notes.A: Transduction is the conversion of stimuli into neural messages.
distractor_notes.B: Weber's law relates the size of a detectable change to the original stimulus.
distractor_notes.D: Synesthesia is experiencing one sense through another.

dq-0116.question: For Jamal, the number 5 always appears red, and the day Tuesday always tastes like cinnamon. Which of the following terms best describes his experiences?
dq-0116.explanation: Correct: A. Experiencing one sensory system through another is synesthesia.

distractor_notes.B: Sensory adaptation is reduced sensitivity to constant stimuli.
distractor_notes.C: Blindsight is responding to visual stimuli without awareness of seeing.
distractor_notes.D: Prosopagnosia is the inability to recognize faces.

dq-0117.question: When Priya has a bad cold and her nose is blocked, her favorite foods seem to have much less flavor. Which of the following best explains this experience?
dq-0117.explanation: Correct: C. Taste and smell work together, so losing one changes the other, which is sensory interaction.

distractor_notes.A: Sensory adaptation is a decrease in sensitivity to constant stimuli.
distractor_notes.B: Synesthesia is one sense triggering another unrelated sense.
distractor_notes.D: Transduction is converting stimuli into neural messages.

dq-0118.question: At dusk, Lena can see shapes and movement at the edges of her vision, but she cannot tell the colors of objects. Which of the following types of cells is mainly responsible for the vision she has in dim light?
dq-0118.explanation: Correct: B. Rods detect shapes and movement in dim light but not color.

distractor_notes.A: Cones detect color and detail and need brighter light.
distractor_notes.C: Ganglion cells pass visual information toward the brain.
distractor_notes.D: Glial cells support neurons but do not detect light.

dq-0119.question: A researcher finds that three types of cells in the retina respond best to short, medium, and long wavelengths of light. Different combinations of their activity produce the full range of colors people see. Which of the following theories does this finding support?
dq-0119.explanation: Correct: D. Three cone types combining their signals is the core of trichromatic theory.

distractor_notes.A: Opponent-process theory involves paired cells such as red and green.
distractor_notes.B: Weber's law is about detecting differences in stimulus intensity.
distractor_notes.C: Sensory interaction is the way senses influence each other.

dq-0120.question: Ava stares at a green square for thirty seconds and then looks at a white wall. She briefly sees a red square on the wall. Which of the following best explains what she sees?
dq-0120.explanation: Correct: A. Afterimages occur when paired ganglion cells, such as red and green, rebound after fatigue.

distractor_notes.B: Trichromatic theory explains color mixing by three cone types, not afterimages.
distractor_notes.C: Accommodation is the lens changing shape to focus light.
distractor_notes.D: The blind spot is where the optic nerve leaves the eye.

dq-0121.question: A patient can read a book held in her hands without trouble, but she cannot read a road sign across the street. An eye doctor explains that light from far objects focuses in front of her retina. Which of the following conditions does she have?
dq-0121.explanation: Correct: D. Clear near vision and blurry distance vision describes nearsightedness.

distractor_notes.A: Farsightedness makes close objects blurry, the opposite pattern.
distractor_notes.B: Color vision deficiency affects seeing certain colors.
distractor_notes.C: Blindsight is responding to visual stimuli without awareness of seeing.

dq-0122.question: In the diagram, which numbered part is where the optic nerve leaves the eye, creating the blind spot?
dq-0122.explanation: Correct: B. The optic nerve exits at part 2, where there are no rods or cones, so that spot cannot detect light.

distractor_notes.A: Part 1 is the lens.
distractor_notes.C: Part 3 is the retina, which does contain light-sensitive cells.
distractor_notes.D: Part 4 is the fovea, where vision is sharpest.

dq-0123.question: In the diagram, which numbered part changes shape to focus light onto the retina?
dq-0123.explanation: Correct: A. The lens changes shape to focus light onto the retina, a process called accommodation.

distractor_notes.B: Part 2 is where the optic nerve leaves the eye.
distractor_notes.C: Part 3 is the retina, which receives light rather than focusing it.
distractor_notes.D: Part 4 is the fovea, a part of the retina.

dq-0124.question: After damage to part of his occipital lobes, a patient can no longer recognize the faces of his family members, although he sees faces clearly and recognizes his family by their voices. Which of the following conditions does the patient have?
dq-0124.explanation: Correct: C. Being unable to recognize faces despite normal vision is prosopagnosia.

distractor_notes.A: Blindsight is responding to unseen stimuli without awareness.
distractor_notes.B: Aphasia is a language impairment.
distractor_notes.D: Synesthesia is experiencing one sense through another.

dq-0125.question: What is the independent variable in this study?
options: The number of math problems solved
The time of day of the test
The number of hours the students slept
dq-0125.explanation: Correct: D. Dr. Ncube manipulated the hours of sleep, so sleep is the independent variable.

distractor_notes.A: This is the outcome that was measured, the dependent variable.
distractor_notes.B: Random assignment spreads ability across groups; it is not manipulated.
distractor_notes.C: The test was given the next morning for all students.

dq-0126.question: According to the graph, how many more problems did the 8-hour group solve, on average, than the 4-hour group?
dq-0126.explanation: Correct: C. The 8-hour group solved 16 problems and the 4-hour group solved 9, a difference of 7.

distractor_notes.A: 3 is the difference between the 8-hour and 6-hour groups.
distractor_notes.B: 4 is the difference between the 6-hour and 4-hour groups.
distractor_notes.D: 9 is the mean for the 4-hour group, not a difference.

dq-0127.question: Which of the following best explains why the 4-hour group scored lower?
options: Sleep loss can reduce thinking and performance the next day.
Jet lag disrupted the circadian rhythm of the 4-hour group.
Hypnagogic sensations lowered the 4-hour group's math ability.
dq-0127.explanation: Correct: A. Less sleep can impair cognitive performance the next day.

distractor_notes.B: No travel across time zones was involved.
distractor_notes.C: Nothing in the study suggests a sleep disorder.
distractor_notes.D: Hypnagogic sensations occur when falling asleep and do not explain the next day's scores.

dq-0128.question: Why did the same 40 adults take part in all three tests?
options: Person-to-person differences could not explain the changes over time.
Each adult's results could be compared with the results of a placebo group.
It guaranteed that the adults were randomly sampled from all adults.
It kept the light intensity the same at each of the three tests.
dq-0128.explanation: Correct: A. Using the same people in every condition means that differences between individuals cannot explain differences between test times.

distractor_notes.B: There is no placebo group in this design.
distractor_notes.C: Random sampling concerns how adults were chosen, not repeated testing.
distractor_notes.D: The researcher changed the intensity on purpose at each test.
